newsitem.title: FRANCE: SOCCER-LILLE-MARSEILLE FRENCH CUP MATCH ON HOLD.
newsitem.headline: SOCCER-LILLE-MARSEILLE FRENCH CUP MATCH ON HOLD.

text.p: Olympique Marseille -- who seem to spend as much time in court as they do actually playing soccer -- are fast becoming embroiled in what yet could prove to be another drawn out court case -- this time over a French Cup match that failed to take place on Saturday.

Marseille, whose name was dragged through the courts following the infamous Valenciennes bribery scandal in 1993 and subsequent demotion to the French second division, are at the centre of a new row which highlights the ever-increasing clash between sports authorities and civil courts.

The problem began when the draw was made for the first round of the French Cup and Marseille were drawn first out of the hat to play a home tie against Lille. As Marseille's Velodrome Stadium is being refurbished for the 1998 World Cup finals, the match could not be played there.
What followed was a series of decisions taken under rules whose meanings were not clearly defined. Eventually the French soccer federation (FFF) ruled Lille could host the game.

Marseille were unhappy and appealed to the FFF who turned them down, ordering them again to play at Lille. The French Olympic Committee moved in to mediate between Lille and Marseille and confirmed the match should be played in Lille.
The FFF commission of appeal then said the draw should be respected and the match be held in Marseille. And, in a last twist, the FFF board decided the match should be played in Lille.
Marseille, meanwhile, had turned to the civil courts which decided to postpone for a month a decision on the FFF's ruling.

That merely complicated the issue even further as the second round is due to be played in three week's time and a month's wait for the court decision would cause serious disruption to the competition.
Then on Monday the FFF said in a statement they would not make any decision about rescheduling the match before Thursday 23 at the earliest "because of the importance of the decision to be made".

By not turning up for the match, Marseille were facing a five-year exclusion from the French Cup -- but they have also incurred the wrath of FFF president Claude Simonet who told sport's daily l'Equipe on Monday: "I mean to fight so that civil authorities cease to endlessly question decisions taken by sports authorities as regards sports problems.

"Olympique Marseille are habitues of the courts. If we are no longer masters of our competition, we can perhaps look ahead to more sad days," echoed Dominique Bathenay, head of the FFF's French Cup commission.
But the FFF, along with other federations, are actually less and less masters of their own competitions.
The Bosman case, for instance, has forced sports federations to stick to the general working laws in their countries.
The FFF recently disovered new implications of the Bosman case when two young players, Nicolas Anelka and Thierry Henry, chose to sign for Arsenal and Real Madrid.

One FFF rule states that players discovered and trained by a club as youths must sign their first professional contract with the same club. Anelka's and Henry's moves signalled that the rule was no longer valid.
Aware that civil courts were increasingly intruding into the sports field, Simonet said the FFF would take a lot of time to make a final decision in the Marseille case.
"I don't want to make any mistake in front of people who turn to civil courts to solve a sports problem. I want to take time to strengthen the power of sports authorities," he said.
